findings.claim: POST /api/maps/:id/entities and POST /api/maps/:id/generate-entities call `await pool.connect()` OUTSIDE their try block, so a connection-acquisition failure escapes the async handler as an unhandledRejection and kills the whole Node process.
findings.failure_scenario: The Postgres container restarts (or max_connections is briefly exhausted) while an admin saves map entities. `pool.connect()` at index.js:580 rejects before the try block is entered; Express 4.18 does not catch async handler rejections, so the rejection reaches the process. Proven locally on Node 22.19 by injecting a pool whose connect() rejects: the HTTP request never gets a response (client aborts) and, with no unhandledRejection listener installed, the process terminates with a fatal uncaught-rejection trace pointing at index.js:580. Because attachAuthority() binds the WS authority to this same server (index.js:1394), the exit drops every connected player mid-session. index.js:653 has the identical shape.
findings.proposed_fix: Move `const client = await pool.connect()` inside the try block in both routes (initialise `let client = null` outside, and guard `client?.release()` in finally), matching the hardening already applied to backend/src/auth/middleware.js:35-43 for the same failure class. Consider also adding a process-level unhandledRejection handler that logs and responds rather than exiting.
findings.verification: Run the repo-local probe: require backend/src/index.js, __setPool({ query: async () => ({rows:[{token_version:1,role:"admin"}]}), connect: async () => { throw new Error("boom"); } }), then POST /api/maps/1/entities with a valid admin bearer token. Expect (current) process exit with an uncaught rejection at index.js:580; after the fix, expect HTTP 500 and the process still alive.

findings.claim: The three unauthenticated job-status proxies interpolate the raw :jobId path param into a URL path, so an encoded ../ traverses out of /jobs/ and reaches arbitrary GET endpoints on the internal sprite-gen service.
findings.failure_scenario: An unauthenticated caller requests GET /api/entity-jobs/..%2F..%2Fopenapi.json. Express decodes the param to "../../openapi.json"; spriteGen.getJob() builds fetch("http://sprite-gen:8100/jobs/../../openapi.json"); the URL parser normalises it to http://sprite-gen:8100/openapi.json. Confirmed live against localhost:13101 on 2026-07-24: the response was sprite-gen full OpenAPI schema (HTTP 200), and GET /api/tile-jobs/..%2Fcapability returned the host hardware profile. sprite-gen is not otherwise reachable from outside the compose network, and none of these three routes requires a token, so the public API is acting as an open unauthenticated GET proxy into the private service segment. Impact today is internal-API and host-capability disclosure; it becomes remote-trigger the moment sprite-gen gains any GET endpoint with a side effect.
findings.proposed_fix: Validate :jobId against the job-id format before use (e.g. reject anything not matching /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/ with 400) in all three proxies — /api/sprite-jobs/:jobId (745), /api/entity-jobs/:jobId (833), /api/tile-jobs/:jobId (894) — and encodeURIComponent it inside services/spriteGen.js:24 so the escape is closed at both layers. Decide separately whether these three routes should require auth at all.
findings.verification: curl -s "http://localhost:13101/api/tile-jobs/..%2Fcapability" with no Authorization header. Currently returns sprite-gen capability JSON with HTTP 200; after the fix expect HTTP 400 and no proxied body.

findings.claim: item_types.value (an item gold worth) is never written by POST or PUT /api/item-types and has no admin UI field, so every item type created after the merchant migration is permanently worth 0 gold.
findings.failure_scenario: An admin creates a new sword via the Item Types panel. The INSERT at index.js:360 omits the `value` column, so it takes the migration default 0 (backend/migrations/1714440032000_merchant_stock.js:6, notNull default 0). services/merchantStock.js:30 seeds a village base catalog with `WHERE category IN (weapon,armor) AND value > 0`, so the new sword can never appear in any merchant catalog; authority/trade.js:91 reads the same column for the sell price, so a player who loots it sells it for sellPriceFor(0) = 0 gold. There is no API route and no form field that can set `value` — the only remedy is a manual SQL UPDATE. Every item type shipped through the admin UI since that migration is affected.
findings.proposed_fix: Add `value` to the INSERT and UPDATE column lists in POST/PUT /api/item-types, validate it in validateItemType() as a non-negative finite integer (the same shape as the existing stamina_cost check at index.js:318), and add the field to ItemTypesAdmin.jsx. Backfill existing zero-value rows using the same expressions the migration used.
findings.verification: curl -s http://localhost:13101/api/item-types | jq '[.[] | {name, value}]' and confirm every row created through the admin UI has value 0; then create an item type via POST /api/item-types with {"value": 25} and confirm the returned row still reports value 0.

findings.claim: PUT /api/worlds/:id stores entry_spawn as any object without checking it lands inside the world bounds, and chooseSpawn() only checks Number.isFinite, so an out-of-range spawn puts every first-time joiner inside the solid wall ring.
findings.failure_scenario: A world is 24x24 tiles (valid coordinates 0..2400 px). In MapsAdmin the entry-spawn inputs (MapsAdmin.jsx:96-98) are plain number fields with no min/max, so an admin typing 99999 saves entry_spawn {x:99999,y:99999}. index.js:1032 accepts any object and writes it to jsonb unvalidated. On join, mapService.chooseSpawn() (line 588) only tests Number.isFinite and returns it verbatim; authority/server.js:206 uses it with no clamp. stampBounds() marks every tile outside the rectangle as map_wall, so every player joining that entry world for the first time materialises deep inside impassable wall with no in-game way out. The same gap lets a bounds shrink via PUT strand already-persisted world_players positions outside the new ring.
findings.proposed_fix: In PUT /api/worlds/:id validate entry_spawn.x/entry_spawn.y are finite numbers inside (0, width*100) x (0, height*100) and return 400 otherwise; when nextW/nextH shrink, also clamp or clear entry_spawn and any world_players rows now outside the ring. Mirror the min/max on the MapsAdmin inputs.
findings.verification: In the browser: set a bounded world as entry, type 99999 into both entry-spawn fields, Save (expect 400 after the fix; currently 200). Then join that world as a fresh player and confirm whether the avatar appears inside the wall and cannot move in any direction.

findings.claim: Entity types are referenced by NAME (not id) in worlds.allowed_creature_types and world_creatures.type, but PUT /api/entity-types/:id renames freely with no check on those references, silently orphaning them.
findings.failure_scenario: A world has allowed_creature_types ["Goblin"] and creature_count 40. An admin renames the Goblin entity type to "Goblin Scout" in the Entity Types panel. PUT /api/entity-types/:id (index.js:239) updates the row with no referential check. The next POST /api/worlds/:id/creatures runs `SELECT ... FROM entity_types WHERE is_creature = true AND name = ANY($1::text[])` (index.js:1120) with the stale ["Goblin"], matches zero rows, skips the placement block, and returns HTTP 200 {"placed": 0}. The admin sees a success toast and a world with no creatures, with no error surfaced anywhere. The same name coupling applies to the hardcoded GUARD_TYPE = "Village Guard" literal (index.js:1177) used by three DELETE statements: renaming that entity type makes the re-roll `WHERE type <> $2` guard-sparing clause stop matching, so a re-roll wipes every village guard.
findings.proposed_fix: Either block a rename that is referenced (check worlds.allowed_creature_types and world_creatures.type, return 409 with the referencing worlds) or cascade it inside one transaction (UPDATE worlds SET allowed_creature_types, UPDATE world_creatures SET type). Longer term, key allowed_creature_types and world_creatures.type on entity_types.id instead of name, and resolve GUARD_TYPE via faction = guard, which is how the authority already identifies guards (authority/creatures.js:66).
findings.verification: With a bounded world configured for one creature type: rename that entity type in the admin UI, then click Re-roll creatures and observe the response. Currently expect HTTP 200 with placed 0 and an empty map; after the fix expect a 409 on the rename or a re-roll that still places creatures.

findings.claim: seedBaseCatalog() is called only at village creation, so item types added later never enter any existing village merchant catalog and there is no re-seed endpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: An admin creates village V in world W; seedBaseCatalog (index.js:1256) copies the item types that exist at that moment into merchant_stock. The admin then adds a new armour type. services/merchantStock.js fetchShop() reads merchant_stock only, and nothing ever re-runs the seed, so players trading at V never see the new armour — and every village created before the item existed is permanently missing it, while villages created afterwards have it. The only recovery is deleting and recreating the village (which cascades away its buyback rows) or a manual SQL insert.
findings.proposed_fix: Add an idempotent re-seed: an admin route (or a call on item-type create) that inserts the missing base-catalog rows for every village, e.g. the existing SELECT-INSERT plus `AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM merchant_stock ms WHERE ms.village_id = $2 AND ms.item_type_id = item_types.id)`, and a matching delete/price-refresh when an item type is removed or repriced.
findings.verification: Create a village, then create a new weapon item type with value > 0, then read the shop for that village and confirm the new weapon is absent. After the fix it should appear without recreating the village.

findings.claim: Village create, village delete and creature re-roll each perform several dependent writes with no transaction, so a failure part-way leaves the world in a state the API cannot be asked to repair.
findings.failure_scenario: POST /api/worlds/:id/villages runs INSERT villages, then insertVillageGuards, then seedBaseCatalog, then invalidateWorld as four independent statements on the shared pool. If seedBaseCatalog throws (constraint error, transient DB fault), the village row and its guards are already committed but the shop is empty; the client gets HTTP 500 "Failed to create village" and the admin retries — and the retry is rejected with 400 "village overlaps an existing village" from the phantom village they were never told exists. DELETE /api/worlds/:id/villages/:villageId (index.js:1265) and POST /api/worlds/:id/creatures (index.js:1097) have the same shape around the guard wipe: they DELETE every world_creatures row of type Village Guard and then re-insert them, so a failure between the two leaves the world with zero guards and no endpoint that re-derives them except another creature re-roll.
findings.proposed_fix: Check out a client and wrap each of the three routes in BEGIN/COMMIT with ROLLBACK in catch and release in finally, exactly as POST /api/maps/:id/entities (index.js:579) already does — and move the connect() inside the try (see the P0 finding on the same pattern).
findings.verification: Point the backend at a pool whose merchant_stock INSERT fails, POST a village, then GET /api/worlds/:id/villages. Currently the village is listed despite the 500; after the fix the list should be unchanged.

findings.claim: creature_count has no server-side upper bound and the re-roll loop issues one round-trip INSERT per creature and a full generateRegion() per placement attempt, so a large count ties the request and a DB connection up indefinitely.
findings.failure_scenario: The Creatures field in MapsAdmin is <Input type="number" min="0"> with no max (MapsAdmin.jsx:79) and PUT /api/worlds/:id only clamps with Math.max(0, Math.floor(creature_count)) (index.js:1027). An admin typing 500000 and clicking Re-roll creatures makes index.js:1118 loop 500k times, each iteration calling generateRegion() for a 1x1 window up to 40 times (each of those rebuilds worldConfig and recomputes the whole coarse path lattice via collectPathCells), then issuing one individual INSERT per placed creature. The request has no timeout and never returns, holds a pool client for its duration, and grows world_creatures without limit — which the authority then loads into the world sim. POST /api/maps/generate (index.js:537) has the same class of gap: rows/cols default to 100 but are unvalidated, so {"rows":100000,"cols":100000} allocates a 10^10-cell grid and exhausts the heap.
findings.proposed_fix: Clamp creature_count server-side in PUT /api/worlds/:id (e.g. 0..2000, 400 above it) and add a max to the MapsAdmin input; batch the placement INSERTs into a single multi-row statement; hoist worldConfig()/collectPathCells() out of the per-attempt path by sampling a pre-generated region instead of calling generateRegion() per candidate tile. Apply the same numeric clamp to rows/cols in POST /api/maps/generate.
findings.verification: PUT /api/worlds/:id with creature_count 200000 (expect 400 after the fix; currently 200), then POST /api/worlds/:id/creatures and time it. Currently expect no response; after the fix expect a 400 at the PUT.

findings.claim: A 50 MB JSON/urlencoded body limit is installed globally, so it applies to every unauthenticated route, and no global rate limit exists — only /api/auth has one.
findings.failure_scenario: express.json({ limit: "50mb" }) at index.js:18 runs as app-level middleware, before routing and before any auth guard, so it parses bodies for unauthenticated paths too. An unauthenticated client POSTs 50 MB of JSON to /api/health (or any path, including ones with no route); the body is buffered and parsed before the 404 is produced. The only rate limiter in the surface is authRateLimiter() inside auth/routes.js:13, scoped to register/login, and cors() is installed with no origin restriction (index.js:17), so this is reachable from any origin without credentials. A modest number of concurrent such requests drives backend heap growth; because the WS authority shares the process (index.js:1394), a heap exhaustion drops every connected player. No route in this surface needs 50 MB: the largest legitimate body is the map entity array in POST /api/maps/:id/entities.
findings.proposed_fix: Drop the global limit to something small (e.g. 256kb) and apply a larger per-route limit only where it is needed, e.g. app.post("/api/maps/:id/entities", adminGuard, express.json({ limit: "10mb" }), handler). Add a modest global rate limiter in front of the router.
findings.verification: head -c 52000000 /dev/zero | tr "\0" "a" into a JSON string file, then run 20 concurrent unauthenticated `curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data-binary @big.json http://localhost:13101/api/health` and watch the backend container RSS. Currently expect large RSS growth per in-flight request; after the fix expect HTTP 413 immediately.

findings.claim: generateWFC() has no caller anywhere outside its own unit tests, yet the tile_types.valid_neighbors column it is the sole consumer of is still a curated, required field in the Tile Types admin UI.
findings.failure_scenario: generateWFC (mapService.js:1-72) and densityAt (mapService.js:337) have zero non-test references in backend/src or frontend/src; world generation goes through generateWorld/generateRegion instead. mapService.js:47 is the only read of validNeighbors in the codebase. TileTypesAdmin.jsx:583 still renders a full checkbox grid for valid_neighbors, POST/PUT /api/tile-types (index.js:467, 488) still persist it, and getTileTypesMap (index.js:91) still ships it to the client. So an admin who spends time curating adjacency rules for every tile type changes nothing about any generated map, and the UI gives no hint of that. The dead generator also keeps its own test suite green, so a change to hash2/globalValueNoise/worldConfig must keep code no product flow reaches passing.
findings.proposed_fix: Decide the product question, then act on it: either delete generateWFC, densityAt, the valid_neighbors editor and (via migration) the column; or wire generateWorld to honour valid_neighbors so the admin input has an effect. Do not leave the field editable while nothing reads it.
findings.verification: Set valid_neighbors on two tile types so they are mutually exclusive, then POST /api/maps/generate and inspect the returned grid for adjacent occurrences of the two. Currently expect them adjacent (the rule is ignored).

findings.claim: The three generation-job routes and the four approve routes are near-verbatim copies that differ only in a kind string and a default frame count, and one copy has already drifted.
findings.failure_scenario: POST /api/sprite-jobs (718), /api/entity-jobs (808) and /api/tile-jobs (869) are identical 20-line blocks apart from kind and the chosenFrames default (4 vs 1 vs 1), including the tier auto-select fallback and the sprite_sets INSERT — so the jobId validation the security finding calls for, or any concurrency cap on this CPU-bound work, must be written three times to be correct. The four approve routes have already drifted: POST /api/entity-types/:id/image clears sprite = NULL with a comment explaining that the atlas path otherwise keeps winning, while POST /api/tile-types/:id/image (904) leaves sprite populated; that is harmless only because resolveTileVisual gates on render_mode === animated rather than on sprite presence, so it is a trap waiting for the tile renderer to adopt the entity precedence rule. job_id handling also differs: three routes treat it as optional, /api/entity-types/:id/sprite (774) 404s without it.
findings.proposed_fix: Extract one startGenerationJob({ subject, kind, defaultFrames, req, res }) helper for the three job routes and one approveGenerated({ table, mode, ... }) helper for the approve routes, so validation, tier fallback and the sprite/image precedence rule exist once. Make the tile image approval clear sprite the way the entity one does, so the two agree.
findings.verification: After extraction, POST each of the three job routes with a jobless payload and confirm identical validation behaviour; approve a tile image over an existing animated tile and confirm tile_types.sprite is NULL.

findings.claim: The WebSocket message handler dereferences msg.type without checking that the parsed frame is an object, so a frame whose body is the four bytes `null` throws inside an async listener and terminates the whole Node process.
findings.failure_scenario: Any registered account opens ws://localhost:13101/authority?token=<its own valid JWT> and sends the literal frame `null`. JSON.parse("null") returns null without throwing, so the try/catch at server.js:378 does not fire; the very next expression evaluates msg.type and throws "TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'type')". The listener is declared async, so the throw becomes a rejected promise that the ws EventEmitter discards, and Node 22 (the runtime in something2-backend-1) defaults to --unhandled-rejections=throw, turning it into an uncaught exception that exits the process. Reproduced locally on Node v22.19.0 with the identical listener shape: exit code 1 with that exact TypeError. No process-level unhandledRejection or uncaughtException handler exists anywhere in backend/src (grep finds only comments referring to the hazard), and ws.on("error") at server.js:374 does not catch it because this is not a transport error. The Express API is attached to the same http server (index.js:1394), so one 4-byte frame from any player drops every connected player and every in-flight HTTP request.
findings.proposed_fix: Guard the envelope before dispatch: immediately after the JSON.parse try/catch at server.js:378 add `if (!msg || typeof msg !== "object" || Array.isArray(msg)) return;`. Additionally wrap the whole message body in a try/catch, mirroring the upgrade handler's `(async () => { ... })().catch(...)` pattern at server.js:114-147, so no future handler branch can escape as an unhandled rejection, and register a process-level unhandledRejection logger as a backstop.
findings.verification: With a valid player JWT: node -e "const W=require('ws');const s=new W('ws://localhost:13101/authority?token=<TOKEN>');s.on('open',()=>s.send('null'))". Currently expect docker logs something2-backend-1 to show the TypeError and the container to exit/restart, dropping every other socket; after the fix expect the frame to be ignored and the socket to stay open.

findings.claim: grantStartingLoadout is gated on "this account owns zero items", which is a state the player can re-enter at will, so reconnecting after emptying the inventory mints a fresh dagger and leather-vest every time.
findings.failure_scenario: A player joins, unequips both starting items and sends two `drop` frames. dropItem (loot.js:218) DELETEs both player_items rows, so the account now owns nothing while both items lie on the ground with a 10-minute TTL. The player closes the socket and reconnects: server.js:415 sees inv.items.length === 0 and calls grantStartingLoadout, whose only guard is `SELECT id FROM player_items WHERE user_id = $1 LIMIT 1` (items.js:92), so it inserts a fresh dagger and leather-vest. The player walks back and picks up the originals: net +2 items per reconnect, unbounded, needing nothing but a page reload. The same loop pays cash without the ground-item step: the live catalog has dagger value 26 and leather-vest value 16 (confirmed via GET /api/item-types on localhost:13101), so selling both to a village merchant credits floor(26/2) + floor(16/2) = 21 gold via sellItem (trade.js:95) and leaves the account at zero items, ready for the next join to re-grant. Gold buys anything in the village base catalog (merchantStock.js:29), so this is unbounded item and currency generation available to every account.
findings.proposed_fix: Make the grant once-per-account rather than once-per-empty-inventory: record it on the account (a users.starting_loadout_granted_at column, or a player_grants row) and gate on that, inside a single statement so two concurrent joins cannot both grant. If a genuine "re-kit a destitute player" behaviour is wanted, make it an explicit and rate-limited action rather than a side effect of join.
findings.verification: In the browser: note the gold total, unequip and sell the starting dagger and leather-vest to a village merchant, reload the page to reconnect, and open the inventory. Currently expect a fresh dagger and leather-vest plus gold up by 21; repeat once to confirm it is unbounded. After the fix expect an empty inventory on the second join.

findings.claim: join passes the client's raw world_id straight into the in-memory worlds Map key, and Postgres accepts several spellings of the same UUID, so a client can conjure a second private simulation of a world and become invisible and untargetable to everyone in the real one.
findings.failure_scenario: worlds.id is a uuid column (migration 1714440012000_create_worlds_and_chunks.js:3). loadWorld(msg.world_id) at server.js:388/150 looks the client string up in the worlds Map by JavaScript identity and, on a miss, runs SELECT ... FROM worlds WHERE id = $1. Postgres uuid input is case-insensitive and also accepts braced and hyphenless forms — verified against something2-db-1: 'A0EEBC99-9C0B-4EF8-BB6D-6BB9BD380A11'::uuid, '{a0eebc99-...}'::uuid and 'a0eebc999c0b4ef8bb6d6bb9bd380a11'::uuid all compare equal to the canonical form. So a client that sends its world id upper-cased gets a Map miss, a successful row fetch, and a SECOND worlds entry backed by the same database world. entry.sockets and world.players are per-entry, so the tick loop's state broadcast (server.js:832) never lists that player for anyone in the canonical entry and never lists anyone else for them: they are invisible and cannot be hit by melee or projectiles, while still killing the same world_creatures rows and looting the same world_items. Both entries also simulate and flushAndPrune-persist the same creature rows independently, so a creature killed in one shard keeps chasing and damaging players in the other and yields no loot when killed there (commitCreatureDeath's DELETE returns rowCount 0). Nothing normalises the value on any path: ws.worldId, persist(), pendingArrivals and evictWorld all key on the same client-supplied string.
findings.proposed_fix: Key the worlds Map on the id RETURNED by loadWorld's SELECT rather than on the client's string, and set ws.worldId from that canonical value — this is the smallest change and also fixes every other worlds.get(ws.worldId) call site. Alternatively reject a world_id that is not the canonical lowercase hyphenated UUID form with a { type: "error" } reply, as part of the envelope validation this handler lacks.
findings.verification: With two player accounts and one real world id: have account A send {"type":"join","world_id":"<id>"} and account B send {"type":"join","world_id":"<the same id upper-cased>"}, then walk both onto the same tile. Currently expect neither state frame to list the other player and melee swings to connect with nothing; after the fix expect both to appear in each other's state frames.

findings.claim: The WebSocketServer is constructed with no maxPayload and no handler applies any rate limit or queue bound, so a single authenticated socket can force 100 MiB allocations per frame and queue unbounded database work.
findings.failure_scenario: new WebSocketServer({ noServer: true }) at server.js:103 inherits ws 8.21.1's default maxPayload of 104857600 bytes (backend/node_modules/ws/lib/websocket-server.js:74). One authenticated player can therefore send repeated ~100 MiB text frames; ws buffers each one, converts it to a string, and hands it to JSON.parse at server.js:378, so a handful of concurrent frames exhausts the container heap and the process is OOM-killed, dropping every player and the co-hosted HTTP API with it. A cheaper variant needs no large frames at all: every mutating handler appends to ws._opChain (server.js:495, 564, 583, 615, 652, 677) with no depth bound, and each link performs at least one database round trip — interact performs two, one of them a DELETE against merchant_stock (merchantStock.js:37). A client that streams {"type":"interact"} frames faster than the chain drains (tens of thousands per second arriving against roughly a thousand round trips per second completing) grows an ever-deeper promise chain of retained closures while monopolising a pool connection, so resident memory climbs monotonically and other players' merchant reads contend on the same table indefinitely. Nothing anywhere in the authority counts, sizes or throttles inbound frames.
findings.proposed_fix: Pass an explicit maxPayload to the WebSocketServer sized to the largest legitimate frame (a join frame is well under 1 KB; 4096 is generous), so an oversized frame closes the socket with code 1009 before it is buffered. Add a per-socket token bucket checked before dispatch, and bound ws._opChain by tracking its depth and refusing new work above a small limit instead of queueing it.
findings.verification: With a valid player JWT, send one 100 MiB frame while watching docker stats something2-backend-1, then send 50000 {"type":"interact"} frames in a burst while watching RSS and SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity. Currently expect RSS to climb by roughly the frame size and to keep climbing under the burst; after the fix expect the oversized frame to close the socket with 1009 and the burst to be dropped at a fixed rate.

findings.claim: dropItem DELETEs the inventory row and INSERTs the ground item as two independent pool.query calls with no transaction, so a failure between them destroys the item permanently.
findings.failure_scenario: dropItem runs DELETE FROM player_items ... RETURNING (loot.js:218) and then INSERT INTO world_items ... (loot.js:225) directly on the pool, which means two connections and two implicit transactions. If the second fails the first is already committed and there is no compensating insert: the item is gone from the account and never reaches the ground. This is reachable without a database outage — world_items.world_id is NOT NULL REFERENCES worlds ON DELETE CASCADE (migration 1714440018000_create_loot.js:16), so an admin deleting a world while a player is still connected to it makes every subsequent drop in that session raise a foreign-key violation; the catch at server.js:620 logs and replies {"type":"error","message":"drop failed"} while the player_items row has already been deleted, and the client shows an error for an item it no longer owns and can never recover. A pool timeout or a database restart in that same window has the identical outcome. The sibling money paths in this surface already do it correctly: buyStock and sellItem (trade.js:12-66 and 76-113) each take a client and wrap the pair in BEGIN/COMMIT, and both claim paths are single-statement CTEs (loot.js:119 and 158), so dropItem is the one remaining split mutation.
findings.proposed_fix: Express both halves as one statement with a CTE, matching claimItem: WITH d AS (DELETE FROM player_items WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2 RETURNING item_type_id, quantity) INSERT INTO world_items (...) SELECT ... FROM d RETURNING ... . That needs no extra connection and makes the pair atomic by construction. Wrapping the existing two statements in a client-scoped BEGIN/COMMIT, as sellItem does, is the equivalent alternative.
findings.verification: Point the authority at a pool whose INSERT INTO world_items rejects (or delete the world row from under a live session) and send a drop frame; then run SELECT count(*) FROM player_items WHERE id = '<itemId>' and SELECT count(*) FROM world_items WHERE world_id = '<world>'. Currently expect 0 and 0 — the item exists nowhere; after the fix expect 1 and 0, with the drop rolled back.

findings.claim: evictWorld refuses to evict a world that has live sockets and returns false, and every admin caller discards that boolean, so world-content edits silently fail to reach exactly the worlds people are playing in.
findings.failure_scenario: A loaded world entry snapshots row, tileTypes, creatureTypes, itemTypes, links and villages once in loadWorld (server.js:150-194) and is only ever dropped when the last player leaves (server.js:715) or by evictWorld. evictWorld returns false without doing anything when entry.sockets.size > 0 (server.js:916), and all four callers — index.js:1064, 1089, 1146 and invalidateWorld at index.js:1172 — ignore the return value. So POST /api/worlds/:id/creatures on a world with even one player online DELETEs and re-INSERTs world_creatures (index.js:1110, 1133) while the live sim keeps its old in-memory creature objects: those players keep fighting creatures that no longer exist in the database, and each kill calls commitCreatureDeath, whose DELETE ... RETURNING matches nothing (loot.js:48-51, rowCount 0), so it returns early and awards no drops and no gold at all. The route replies 200 {"placed": N} and the admin sees success. The same staleness applies to villages and links: creating a village with a merchant via POST /api/worlds/:id/villages leaves entry.villages empty, so interact at the new merchant answers "no merchant nearby" indefinitely and planBind never binds a respawn point, with nothing anywhere reporting why. activateChunk does not rescue this, because it skips any chunk already in loadedChunks.
findings.proposed_fix: Give the authority a refresh path that re-reads row, links and villages and reconciles the creature set in place, and call it from the same admin mutations instead of relying on eviction; keep evictWorld for the idle case. At minimum, propagate the refusal: have the admin routes read the boolean and report to the caller that the change will not take effect until the world empties, so a re-roll that did nothing does not present as a success.
findings.verification: With one player connected to a bounded world, re-roll that world's creatures from the admin UI, then have the player kill a creature it can still see. Currently expect no drop and no gold, and SELECT count(*), min(x) FROM world_creatures WHERE world_id = '<id>' to disagree with what the player is looking at; after the fix expect the player's creature set to match the database.

findings.claim: activateChunk uses the world_chunks INSERT as its once-only spawn flag but commits it before the rest of the activation, so a transient failure afterwards leaves that chunk permanently free of wild creatures — and the empty catch means nothing is logged.
findings.failure_scenario: activateChunk (server.js:247-300) runs INSERT INTO world_chunks ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id and uses ins.rowCount > 0 as the guard for spawnChunkCreatures (server.js:262). Every statement in the function is its own transaction. If any later statement throws — a per-creature INSERT, the creature SELECT, the world_items SELECT — control reaches the bare catch at server.js:295, which logs nothing, and the chunk is deliberately left out of loadedChunks so recomputeActive (server.js:315, every 4 ticks, roughly 200 ms) retries it. But on every retry the world_chunks row now exists, ins.rowCount is 0, and the creature-spawn block is skipped. The chunk is therefore permanently empty of wild creatures in any unbounded world, and no amount of retrying, rejoining or restarting the server recovers it — the only remedy is deleting the world_chunks row by hand. Because the catch is silent, the operator sees neither the original error nor the 5 Hz retry loop it starts, and a player standing in that chunk simply sees a world with nothing in it.
findings.proposed_fix: Make materialisation and spawning one unit of work: take a client and wrap the world_chunks INSERT together with the creature INSERTs in a single BEGIN/COMMIT, so a failure rolls the world_chunks row back and the retry genuinely retries. Independently, log the swallowed error at server.js:295 (console.error("chunk activation failed:", chunkKey, err)) so the condition is visible at all, and add a backoff so a persistently failing chunk is not re-attempted five times a second.
findings.verification: Inject a pool whose INSERT INTO world_creatures rejects exactly once, activate a fresh chunk in an unbounded world, let the next retry succeed, then run SELECT count(*) FROM world_creatures WHERE world_id = '<id>' AND x >= <chunk x0> AND x < <chunk x1>. Currently expect 0 permanently; after the fix expect the retry to spawn that chunk's creatures.

findings.claim: buyStock looks the stock row up by id alone — it never checks that the row belongs to the village the player is standing at, to the world they are in, or that it has not expired — so the "no merchant nearby" gate does not constrain what can actually be bought.
findings.failure_scenario: The buy handler (server.js:657) only asserts that SOME merchant is within INTERACT_RADIUS and then discards the village it found, passing only msg.stockId to buyStock, which selects WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE (trade.js:17) and reads village_id into a variable it never compares against anything. A player who has once opened village A's shop — the shop frame at server.js:639 hands them every row id — can then walk to village B, or travel through a doorway into a different world entirely, and buy A's unique player-buyback listings from B's merchant, taking an item out of a village they are not in and cannot currently reach. The same missing predicate makes expired listings purchasable: expires_at is only swept lazily per village by fetchShop (merchantStock.js:37-40) and buyStock has no expires_at predicate at all, so a buyback row whose 3-day window has lapsed still sells as long as nobody has opened that village's shop since it expired. Stock ids are UUIDs so this is not blind guessing, but it makes the physical-merchant model advisory rather than enforced, which is the entire premise of villages. The sell handler at server.js:684 already passes village.id through; buy is the one that does not.
findings.proposed_fix: Pass the village resolved by nearestMerchantVillage into buyStock the way the sell handler already does, and add AND village_id = $2 AND world_id = $3 AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > now()) to the FOR UPDATE select, so the row's location and validity are decided inside the same locked read that decides the sale.
findings.verification: With two villages that both have merchants, open village A's shop and record a buyback row's stockId, then stand at village B's merchant and send {"type":"buy","stockId":"<A's id>"}. Currently expect a bought frame and the row to vanish from A's catalog; after the fix expect {"type":"error","message":"that item is no longer for sale"} and the row still listed in A.

findings.claim: The socket message handler is a 320-line if-chain in which every branch invents its own guards, so input validation is applied inconsistently and the gaps are where this surface's two worst defects live.
findings.failure_scenario: server.js:376-698 dispatches eleven message types with no shared envelope validation and no per-type argument spec. The inconsistency is already in the tree: drop, buy and sell type-check their id (typeof msg.itemId !== "string" at 614, 651, 676), while equip and unequip pass msg.itemId and msg.slot straight through, pickup and interact check nothing, and join neither validates nor normalises msg.world_id. No branch checks that the frame is an object at all. Those last two gaps are not hypothetical: they are the process-killing `null` frame and the duplicate-world-shard exploit filed separately against this same handler, and one validated dispatch point would have closed both. The ongoing cost is that any cross-cutting concern — per-type rate limiting, a protocol version, an audit log of client commands, a per-type auth check — currently means eleven independent edits with eleven chances to miss one, which is exactly how the present inconsistency arose. Six of the branches also repeat the identical ws._opChain serialisation-plus-try/catch boilerplate verbatim.
findings.proposed_fix: Replace the if-chain with a dispatch table keyed on msg.type, each entry declaring its handler plus a small argument spec (types, and an id format where applicable), and validate the envelope once before dispatch — msg is a plain object and msg.type is a known string. Handlers then receive already-validated values, and the ws._opChain wrapper repeated in six branches becomes one shared decorator rather than six copies.
findings.verification: Structural. After the change, assert that for each message type a frame with a wrong-typed field is rejected uniformly, and that the frames null, [], 1 and "x" are all ignored without reaching any handler.

findings.claim: The token-revocation check — SELECT token_version, compare against the JWT's tv — exists in two independent copies, one in the HTTP middleware and one in the WS upgrade handler, with no test asserting they agree.
findings.failure_scenario: Both copies read token_version and reject when it differs from payload.tv (auth/middleware.js:37-46 and authority/server.js:134-136). They agree today and nothing is currently broken, which is why this is recorded at P3 rather than higher. The cost is prospective and specific: any second revocation condition has to be added in both places. Adding a ban or disabled flag, an issued-at floor, or a move to a session table means editing two files whose SELECT lists have already diverged (the middleware also selects role; the WS query does not), and a change applied only to the HTTP copy would leave a banned account's live game socket running until it disconnects — which is precisely the failure the WS copy exists to prevent.
findings.proposed_fix: Extract the check into one exported helper in backend/src/auth (for example assertTokenCurrent(pool, payload) returning the user row or null) and have both callers use it, keeping their transport-specific responses — 401 JSON versus socket.destroy() — at the call sites.
findings.verification: Not statically checkable. After extraction, one test that bumps a user's token_version and asserts both an HTTP request and a live WS upgrade are rejected covers both call sites, which no current test does.

findings.claim: player_items.quantity is read and preserved by four code paths but written above 1 by none, and sellItem silently destroys any surplus if a stack ever appears.
findings.failure_scenario: consumeAmmo and ammoCount (ammo.js:37 and 67) are built entirely around multi-unit stacks, claimItem copies world_items.quantity into the inventory row (loot.js:120) and dropItem carries it back out (loot.js:229) — but every INSERT into player_items in the tree writes quantity 1 or the column default: trade.js:40, items.js:100, index.js:424, and spawnDrops, which deliberately inserts one ground item per unit rolled (loot.js:72-82). SELECT count(*) FROM player_items WHERE quantity > 1 on the live game_db returns 0. So the ammo module's central design decision — the pick CTE and its long comment about stacks never being merged — is defending a state that nothing produces. The trap it leaves is in sellItem (trade.js:81-101): it DELETEs the whole row regardless of quantity, pays sellPriceFor(value) for a single unit, and lists exactly one buyback item, so the first write path that ever creates a stack turns selling it into a silent loss of every unit but one.
findings.proposed_fix: Decide the question once. Either remove the stacking machinery — pin player_items.quantity at 1 and reduce consumeAmmo to a single-row delete — or make stacks real, merging on grant and making sellItem price and list quantity units (or refuse to sell a stack). Leaving both halves half-built is what makes the sell path a latent data-loss bug.
findings.verification: SELECT count(*) FROM player_items WHERE quantity > 1 on game_db, currently 0. Then in a scratch database set one row to quantity 5, sell it to a merchant, and confirm the player is paid for one unit while all five are destroyed.

findings.claim: MapsAdmin destructures only {worlds, isLoadingWorlds} from useWorlds() and never reads worldsError, so a failed /api/worlds fetch renders the same "no maps yet" empty state as a genuinely empty catalog.
findings.failure_scenario: An admin's session token has been revoked (password rotated, logout-everywhere) or the network blips while the Maps tab is open. useWorlds() (useWorlds.js:10-18) sets worldsError from the query, and its own comment says "errors are surfaced via the returned error and toasted by the caller" — Something2.jsx honors that contract (Something2.jsx:396-402, toasts worldsError), but MapsAdmin.jsx:153 does not. isLoadingWorlds flips to false, worlds stays undefined, boundedMaps becomes [], and MapsAdmin renders "No bounded maps yet. Generate one above." with zero indication anything failed. The admin, seeing an apparently-empty catalog, may click "Generate map" and create a duplicate of a map that still exists server-side but simply failed to load.
findings.proposed_fix: Destructure worldsError from useWorlds() in MapsAdmin.jsx and toast it in a useEffect, mirroring the pattern already used in Something2.jsx (lines 400-402), or better, lift that effect into useWorlds() itself so every caller gets it for free instead of each one having to remember to opt in.
findings.verification: In the browser, open the Maps admin tab, then force /api/worlds to fail (revoke the token via `make admin-password` in another tab, or block the request in devtools) and reload the tab. Expect an error toast and a visibly-different state from "no maps yet"; currently expect the empty-state message with no toast.

findings.claim: useCreateEntityType/useUpdateEntityType/useDeleteEntityType and useCreateTileType/useUpdateTileType/useDeleteTileType throw a hardcoded generic Error string on a non-ok response, discarding the backend's {error: "..."} body, while the otherwise-identical useCreateItemType/useUpdateItemType/useDeleteItemType (useMaps.js:291-349) parse that same body and surface the real message.
findings.failure_scenario: Two admins have the Entity Types tab open. Admin A opens Edit on "Goblin". Admin B deletes "Goblin" in their own tab. Admin A edits a stat and clicks Save Changes: PUT /api/entity-types/:id returns 404 {"error":"Entity type not found"} (index.js:264), but useUpdateEntityType (useMaps.js:230-248) ignores the body and throws the fixed string "Failed to update entity type", so the toast reads "Update failed: Failed to update entity type" — it never tells Admin A the row is gone and a refresh is needed. Running the identical race in the Item Types tab shows "Update failed: Item type not found" (useUpdateItemType parses error.error at useMaps.js:315-319), which is actually actionable.
findings.proposed_fix: Give useCreateEntityType/useUpdateEntityType/useDeleteEntityType and the three tile-type mutations the same res.json().catch(()=>({})) parse-and-throw pattern already used by the item-type mutations, or extract one shared apiMutationError(res) helper so the four catalogs cannot drift again.
findings.verification: With two browser tabs signed in as admin: in tab 1 open Edit on an entity type, in tab 2 delete that same entity type, then in tab 1 click Save Changes. Expect the toast to name the real reason ("Entity type not found"); currently expect the generic "Failed to update entity type".

findings.claim: EntityTypesAdmin and TileTypesAdmin only validate that name is non-empty before submitting, while the sibling ItemTypesAdmin mirrors the backend's category-aware validateItemType() (validateClient(), ItemTypesAdmin.jsx:372-396) — and the backend for entity-types/tile-types has no equivalent bounds check either (index.js:208-237, 457-475 only check `!name || !color`), so stats like hp, max_hp, mana, strength and chance can be saved negative or nonsensical with no error anywhere.
findings.failure_scenario: An admin editing a creature entity type mistypes Max HP as -50 (EntityTypesAdmin.jsx:1049-1050, a bare <input type="number"> with no min/max and no client check). handleSubmit (line 819) only checks formData.name.trim(); it saves. PUT /api/entity-types/:id (index.js:239-270) writes max_hp=-50 verbatim with no server-side validation either. The row now persists a negative max HP with no error ever shown to the admin, unlike the Item Types form, which would have rejected an equally invalid weapon/armor/ammo combination client-side before the request was even sent.
findings.proposed_fix: Add a validateClient()-style check to EntityTypesAdmin and TileTypesAdmin (at minimum: numeric stats >= 0, chance in [0,1], speed in [0,2]) mirroring the pattern ItemTypesAdmin already established, and add the matching server-side check in index.js so the gap is closed on both sides rather than just the one panel that happens to have it.
findings.verification: In the Entity Types admin, edit an entity and set Max HP to -50, click Save Changes. Expect a client-side validation error naming the field; currently expect the save to succeed silently.

findings.claim: MapPreview.jsx and the legacy flat-map hooks it depends on (useMaps, fetchMap, fetchMapEntities, useGenerateMap, useDeleteMap, useSaveEntities, useGenerateEntities — all in useMaps.js) have zero call sites anywhere in the frontend; the whole "maps" subsystem was superseded by the worlds/chunked system (useWorlds.js, MapsAdmin.jsx) but was never removed.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer greps for "map preview" or "generate map" while extending the admin UI, finds MapPreview.jsx and useGenerateMap looking like a complete, working feature (styled, commented, animated), and wires a new screen to them assuming they are the supported path. It would call the legacy /api/maps/generate and /api/maps/:id endpoints (index.js:158,520,535,560,579,624,651), producing a map that lives in the old `maps` table and never appears in MapsAdmin.jsx's boundedMaps list or the world picker in Something2.jsx, because both only read from /api/worlds. The map looks like it silently vanished.
findings.proposed_fix: Delete MapPreview.jsx and the unused legacy exports from useMaps.js (useMaps, fetchMap, fetchMapEntities, useGenerateMap, useDeleteMap, useSaveEntities, useGenerateEntities) together with their backend routes, or if the flat-map system is still needed for some path this audit did not find, wire at least one admin entry point to it so it is not silently unreachable.
findings.verification: grep -rn "MapPreview\|useGenerateMap\|useDeleteMap\b\|useSaveEntities\|fetchMap(\|fetchMapEntities" frontend/src --include=*.jsx --include=*.js, excluding the defining files themselves; expect zero matches, confirming nothing renders or calls these today.

findings.claim: TileTypesAdmin's delete has no check for whether an entity type's spawn_tiles references the tile being deleted, and EntityTypesAdmin's Spawn Tiles multi-select (line 1064-1075) only renders checkboxes for tiles currently in tileTypes, so a dangling spawn_tiles entry left behind by a tile deletion becomes permanently invisible and un-removable through the admin UI.
findings.failure_scenario: An admin creates entity type "Cactus" with spawn_tiles ["sand"], then later deletes the "sand" tile type from the Tile Types tab (TileTypesAdmin.jsx:432-436, a bare window.confirm with no reference check; DELETE /api/tile-types/:id has no FK/consistency guard either, index.js:503-517). entity_types.spawn_tiles is untouched jsonb, so the "Cactus" row still contains ["sand"]. Reopening Cactus in EntityTypesAdmin, the Spawn Tiles MultiSelect only iterates the live tileTypes list (line 1065), so the checkbox for "sand" no longer exists — the admin cannot see or uncheck it. Any Save Changes on that entity re-sends the untouched formData.spawn_tiles array, so the dead reference persists indefinitely, invisible in the UI that is supposed to be its source of truth.
findings.proposed_fix: Before deleting a tile type, query which entity types reference it in spawn_tiles (and vice versa for valid_neighbors) and either block the delete with a 409 listing the referencing rows, or cascade-strip the name from those arrays in the same request; at minimum, have EntityTypesAdmin render orphaned spawn_tiles entries (e.g. greyed out with a "tile no longer exists" note and a way to remove them) instead of silently dropping them from the visible list.
findings.verification: Create an entity type with a spawn tile checked, delete that tile type from the Tile Types tab, then reopen the entity type's edit modal. Expect either a warning about the dangling reference or a way to clear it; currently expect the Spawn Tiles list to simply omit it with no indication anything is wrong.

findings.claim: WorldAuthorityClient's onClose handler only sets `this.authorityJoined = false` (a field nothing else in the codebase reads) — there is no reconnect attempt, no heartbeat (WorldAuthorityClient.ping() is defined at net/WorldAuthorityClient.js:122 but is never called by any caller in the client), and no state transition to alert the player, unlike the deliberate 'kicked' flow at Game.js:374-378 which does call setState('kicked').
findings.failure_scenario: The backend authority process restarts (deploy, crash, or a transient network blip) while a player is mid-session. The WebSocket 'close' event fires WorldAuthorityClient.onClose, which only flips the unused `authorityJoined` flag; Game.state stays 'playing' and the rAF loop keeps calling update()/render() every frame, so the player's sprite keeps moving under local prediction (Player.update against the already-loaded chunkedMap) and the screen looks fully live. Every subsequent authorityClient.sendAttack/sendEquip/sendPickup/sendInteract/sendBuy/sendSell call now hits WorldAuthorityClient._send's `if (!this.ws || this.ws.readyState !== WebSocket.OPEN) return false` guard and is silently dropped — no toast, no error, no retry — because none of Game.js's input handlers (setupInput, _handleInventoryClick, _handleShopClick) check that return value. The player has no way to tell the session died except that other players stop appearing or moving, and the only recovery is a manual page reload.
findings.proposed_fix: Add a heartbeat (call the existing but unused ping()) and treat a non-intentional close (this._closed === false at the point onClose fires) as fatal: transition Game to a visible 'disconnected' state (mirroring the existing 'kicked' render branch at Game.js:597-609) and either auto-reconnect authorityClient with backoff or show a clear 'connection lost — reload' message instead of leaving the player in a silently-broken 'playing' state.
findings.verification: In the browser: join a chunked world, then force-close the authority WebSocket (devtools Network tab, or kill/restart the authority server process). Confirm the player sprite keeps responding to WASD with no on-screen indication anything is wrong, and that pressing 'g'/'e' or left-clicking to attack produces no toast and no visible error — only a manual reload restores play.

findings.claim: renderChunked's tile-draw loop iterates every cell chunkTileCells (core/chunkTiles.js:38-60) returns — which culls only at whole-CHUNK granularity via chunkVisible — and calls worldToScreen plus allocates a cell object for EVERY tile of every chunk-visible chunk, before RenderSystem.js:123's per-tile relX/relY bounds check throws most of them away. With the backend's default chunkSize of 64 (backend/src/authority/world.js:81) and ChunkStreamer's radius of 1 (core/Game.js:290 -> 9 loaded chunks), that is up to 9*64*64 = 36864 worldToScreen calls and object allocations rebuilt from scratch every single animation frame.
findings.failure_scenario: On the fixed 1280x720 canvas (GAME_WIDTH/HEIGHT) with 128x64 iso diamonds (ISO_TILE_W/H), well under a thousand tiles are ever actually on screen, but chunkTileCells enumerates and projects all ~36864 loaded-and-chunk-visible cells every frame at 60fps before the bulk are discarded by the per-tile cull at RenderSystem.js:123 — over an order of magnitude more worldToScreen calls and array pushes than the frame needs, with the array itself reallocated fresh every frame. This is the dominant avoidable per-frame cost in the render path and gets strictly worse the moment chunkSize or the streamer radius is increased, or on lower-end/mobile hardware, directly lowering frame rate during ordinary movement rather than during any one heavy action.
findings.proposed_fix: Push the existing per-tile relX/relY visibility check (RenderSystem.js:123) down into chunkTileCells itself (or compute a cheap local row/col range per visible chunk from the camera bounds) so off-screen cells are never constructed or projected in the first place — chunkVisible already proves this exact pattern one granularity up (chunk-level) and it just needs to be repeated at tile-level.
findings.verification: In the browser with devtools Performance recording, join a chunked world and walk continuously; compare the cell count chunkTileCells produces for a frame against the count that survives the RenderSystem.js:123 per-tile cull for that same frame, and measure time spent inside renderChunked's tile loop.

findings.claim: Game.js's entire non-chunked code path — init() (210-250), setMap() (252-254), the non-chunked branches of update()/render() (462-472, 651-653), _onServerState()/_reconcileSelf() (479-579, including the RECONCILE_SOFT_PX/HARD_PX/LERP tuning constants at 44-46) — plus net/EngineClient.js's WebSocket-wrapper class (lines 19-131 only, not the auth helper functions below it which ARE used elsewhere), core/Map.js (264 lines), entities/MapEntity.js, and the 'legacy single-Map path' branch of Player.update (entities/Player.js:56-125) are never reached by the shipped app: Something2.jsx never calls Game.prototype.init, never calls setEngineClient with a real client (only the teardown call `setEngineClient?.(null, null)` at Something2.jsx:461), and never does `new EngineClient(...)` anywhere in frontend/src (confirmed by repo-wide grep). No test file calls Game.prototype.init, setEngineClient, or instantiates the EngineClient WS-wrapper class either.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer, reading Game.js's own inline comments describing dual chunked/non-chunked support, spends time tuning RECONCILE_SOFT_PX/RECONCILE_HARD_PX/RECONCILE_LERP (Game.js:44-46) or fixing a suspected bug in _reconcileSelf (Game.js:562-579) to smooth out perceived player rubber-banding in production — but that code path only executes via _onServerState, which only fires from an EngineClient instance that Something2.jsx never creates, so the change has zero effect on any real session; the actual live reconciliation path is net/reconcile.js via _onWorldState, an entirely separate implementation with its own tuning. The same trap applies to anyone patching core/Map.js's collision/tile logic or Player.js's non-ChunkedMap branch believing it still backs some reachable in-game mode: the fix ships, the tests (if any are added against the dead path) pass, and no real player is ever affected because the code never runs.
findings.proposed_fix: Delete the unreachable branches: Game.init/setMap/_onServerState/_reconcileSelf and their RECONCILE_* constants, the EngineClient WS-wrapper class (relocate the still-used auth helper functions below it into their own module first), core/Map.js, entities/MapEntity.js, and Player.update's legacy branch. This removes roughly 500 lines split across Game.js/Player.js/Map.js/EngineClient.js, directly shrinking Game.js and Player.js without touching any code that actually executes, and removes the risk of a future change being made against a path with no effect.
findings.verification: Repo-wide grep confirms no reachable call site: `grep -rn "new EngineClient(" frontend/src` returns nothing; `grep -rn "setEngineClient" frontend/src/games/something2/Something2.jsx` shows only the `(null, null)` teardown call; `grep -rln "\.init(\|setEngineClient\|new EngineClient" frontend/src/games/something2/src/js` returns only core/Game.js itself (the definition site, not a caller).

findings.claim: The 't' (toggle tile textures, Game.js:786-789) and 'm' (cycle render-mode override, Game.js:780-783) dev keydown handlers are missing the `!e.repeat` guard that every other one-shot hotkey in the same setupInput() method already uses ('i' at 739, 'e' at 761, 'g' at 773), so they re-fire on every OS auto-repeat tick while the key is held rather than once per physical key press.
findings.failure_scenario: A developer holds 't' down instead of tapping it (even the OS default key-repeat window, typically starting after ~500ms and repeating every ~30-50ms, is enough): toggleTileTextures() flips on/off many times before keyup, each flip also replacing the on-screen toast via _showToast, and the final rendered state on release is whichever parity the repeat count happened to land on — effectively unpredictable from the user's point of view — unlike every other panel/mode hotkey in this same handler, which fires exactly once per press.
findings.proposed_fix: Add `&& !e.repeat` to both the 't' and 'm' conditions, matching the guard already used for 'i', 'e', and 'g' a few lines above each.
findings.verification: In the browser, press and hold 't' (or 'm') for about a second and release; observe the tile-texture (or render-mode) toggle state after release does not reliably correspond to a single press, and the toast/console log fires repeatedly during the hold.

findings.claim: SPRITE_STORE_ENABLED is a container-wide env flag with no test-mode override, so running the sprite-gen pytest suite inside the deployed container performs real writes to the production MinIO 'sprites' bucket.
findings.failure_scenario: docker exec something2-sprite-gen-1 pytest -q (the project's own baseline command) runs test_object_storage_api.py::test_generate_kind_object_manifest_keys_are_flat, which POSTs creature: 'Tree', kind: 'object' to /generate; because SPRITE_STORE_ENABLED=true is set in this container, main.py's work() calls default_store().put_object('Tree', out) for real and overwrites sprites/objects/Tree/{static.png,atlas.png,atlas.json} in the live MinIO bucket with an 8x8 stub placeholder image — 'Tree' is a real row in entity_types (confirmed via the game_db). The same run's test_tile_storage_api.py::test_generate_kind_tile_runs_tile_branch_no_store POSTs creature: 'grass', kind: 'tile', silently overwriting sprites/tiles/grass/static.png — 'grass' is a real row in tile_types — and this second overwrite causes no test failure at all, because put_tile's returned dict happens to still contain a 'frames' key that satisfies the test's assertion.
findings.proposed_fix: Add a pytest-only guard (e.g. an autouse conftest.py fixture that monkeypatches app.main._STORE_ENABLED to False, or a dedicated test-runner entrypoint that unsets SPRITE_STORE_ENABLED / points MINIO_BUCKET at a disposable test bucket) so the suite can never reach default_store() regardless of the container it runs in.
findings.verification: Note the object timestamp for sprites/tiles/grass/static.png in MinIO, run docker exec something2-sprite-gen-1 pytest -q tests/test_tile_storage_api.py, then confirm the timestamp is unchanged; also confirm app.main._STORE_ENABLED is False inside the pytest process after the fix.

findings.claim: POST /generate has no authentication and no upper bound on frames/steps/size, and JobManager runs jobs on one synchronous worker thread with no timeout or cancellation, so a single call can monopolize the service for hours with no recovery short of restarting the container.
findings.failure_scenario: Any caller able to reach the sprite-gen container's HTTP port — which by default includes every other container on the compose network, since main.py has no auth middleware at all, and compose/docker-compose.yml publishes it as "18100:8100" with no source-IP restriction (Docker binds 0.0.0.0 by default) — POSTs {creature:'x', base_prompt:'y', kind:'creature', frames:500} with no explicit backend. backend_name resolves to sd-turbo (the deployment default, ~66s/frame observed), so 500 frames x 8 directions = 4000 sequential generations queue on the sole JobManager worker (tens of hours); every other /generate call, including the ones the Node backend's own adminGuard-protected routes submit for real admins, sits queued behind it with no cancel path (jobs.py exposes no kill/cancel) until the container is restarted.
findings.proposed_fix: Clamp frames/steps/size to explicit maxima in the GenerateRequest Pydantic model and reject requests over the max with 422 instead of queueing them; add a bounded job queue and a way to cancel/expire a running job; consider a shared-secret header so only the backend container can reach /generate.
findings.verification: POST /generate with frames: 500 and confirm it is rejected with 422 rather than accepted with 202; separately confirm (with the infra audit) whether port 18100 is reachable from outside the compose network.

findings.claim: GenerateRequest.kind is an unconstrained string, so any value other than exactly 'tile' or 'object' silently falls through to the full 8-direction creature pipeline with a different response shape, instead of being rejected.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller sends kind: 'Tile' (capitalized) or any other typo'd/unrecognized value; work()'s `if req.kind == 'tile': ...` and `if req.kind == 'object': ...` both fail to match, so it silently falls through to generate_creature — 8 directions x n_frames instead of the one flat image the caller asked for, roughly 8x the generation time — and the result is stored/returned in put_creature's shape (atlas_key, frame_keys) instead of put_tile/put_object's shape (image_key, frames), so a caller written against the flat shape gets undefined/KeyError reading result['image_key'].
findings.proposed_fix: Change GenerateRequest.kind to Literal['creature', 'tile', 'object'] so FastAPI/Pydantic rejects an unrecognized kind with 422 at the request boundary instead of silently mis-routing it.
findings.verification: POST /generate with kind: 'Tile' and confirm it now returns 422 instead of 202 with a creature-shaped result.

findings.claim: GenerateRequest.size accepts a list of any length with no shape validation, so a malformed size is accepted at 202 and only fails deep inside the async job after real backend compute, instead of being rejected at the request boundary.
findings.failure_scenario: POST /generate with kind: 'tile', no explicit backend (resolves to sd-turbo, this deployment's default) and size: [16] returns 202; the job runs a full ~66s real sd-turbo diffusion pass at the fixed 512x512 native resolution in SDTurboBackend.generate, then crashes on result.images[0].resize((16,), LANCZOS) because PIL's resize requires a 2-tuple — the CPU time is spent before the job ends in status 'error' with a raw Python unpacking/resize exception surfaced verbatim through GET /jobs/{id}.
findings.proposed_fix: Validate size as a 2-element list of positive ints in the Pydantic model (a field validator, or a tuple[int, int] type) so a malformed shape is rejected with 422 before any job is queued.
findings.verification: POST /generate with size: [16] and confirm 422 is returned immediately instead of a queued job that errors out after real generation time.

findings.claim: sd15.py, sd_turbo.py, and sdxl.py each independently implement the same seed-to-torch.Generator construction with the same narrow `except ModuleNotFoundError` catch, and the copies have already drifted: sd_turbo.py extracted its copy into a named _generator() method while sd15.py and sdxl.py still inline theirs directly in generate().
findings.failure_scenario: A fix to broaden the exception handling (e.g. to also catch a torch device-mismatch RuntimeError, which none of the three currently catch and which would otherwise propagate up and fail the job with an unhelpful trace) gets applied to sd_turbo.py's named _generator() method because that is the only place a reviewer sees a function to fix, while the byte-identical inlined logic in sd15.py's and sdxl.py's generate() is missed, leaving two of the three backends with the original gap.
findings.proposed_fix: Extract the shared seed->Generator construction (with its exception handling) into one function in backends/base.py, and have all three backends call it instead of inlining/duplicating it.
findings.verification: Grep for 'except ModuleNotFoundError' across sprite-gen/app/backends/*.py after the fix and confirm it appears exactly once.

findings.claim: The /generate response reports recipe.controlnet/steps/frames from recipe_for(tier) using the requested/detected tier, independent of the backend_name actually resolved for the job, so it can describe a pipeline that never runs.
findings.failure_scenario: SPRITE_BACKEND=sd-turbo is permanently set in compose/docker-compose.yml for this deployment. A caller POSTs {tier: 'gpu', creature: 'goblin', base_prompt: 'x'} with no explicit backend, expecting the gpu-tier sdxl/ControlNet pipeline; backend_name resolves to 'sd-turbo' via the SPRITE_BACKEND override instead (confirmed live: test_generate_fills_defaults_from_tier_recipe now gets backend 'sd-turbo' back instead of the expected 'sdxl'), yet the response's recipe.controlnet is still True and steps is still 30, because those fields come from recipe_for('gpu') rather than from what sd-turbo actually does — SDTurboBackend has no ControlNet pipeline at all and internally clamps steps to 4 — so a caller relying on the response to know whether pose-guided ControlNet generation ran is misled.
findings.proposed_fix: Derive controlnet/steps/frames for the response from the resolved backend_name (e.g. a small per-backend capability table) instead of purely from recipe_for(tier), so the reported recipe always matches what actually executes.
findings.verification: POST /generate with tier: 'gpu' and no backend while SPRITE_BACKEND=sd-turbo is set; confirm the response's controlnet field reads False, matching the backend that will actually run.
